# Linear equations in business {#sec-linear}

::: {.goals}
Goals

- Solve linear equations with brackets and fractions.
- Set up and solve a break-even equation, and explain the contribution margin.
- Find the volume or the price for a target profit.
- Round answers in a way that makes business sense.
:::

The video for this chapter is the second half of **What an equation is, and how to solve linear equations** in @sec-equations.

## Linear equations

An equation is **linear** if the unknown appears only to the first power: no $q^2$, no $\sqrt{q}$, no $q$ in a denominator. Every linear equation can be brought into the form $a \cdot x = b$, and if $a \neq 0$ its only solution is $x = \frac{b}{a}$.

A recipe that always works:

1. Remove brackets by multiplying out.
2. Remove fractions by multiplying both sides by a common denominator.
3. Collect all terms with the unknown on one side and all numbers on the other.
4. Divide by the number in front of the unknown.
5. Check by putting the solution back in.

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: brackets and fractions
Solve $\frac{x}{4} + \frac{x - 2}{6} = 3$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x}{4} + \frac{x - 2}{6} &= 3 &&\mid \cdot 12\\
3x + 2(x - 2) &= 36 &&\text{(multiply out)}\\
3x + 2x - 4 &= 36 &&\mid +4\\
5x &= 40 &&\mid :5\\
x &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Check: $\frac{8}{4} + \frac{6}{6} = 2 + 1 = 3$. ✓ The factor 12 is the smallest number that both 4 and 6 divide.
:::

## Break-even: when does the business stop losing money?

Loop Cycles has **fixed costs** of €2,600 per month: rent, insurance, tools and the website. They have to be paid whether it sells zero bikes or fifty. Each refurbished bike has **variable costs** of €260 (buying the bike, parts and work) and sells for €364 net (@sec-s1-business). Let $q$ be the number of bikes sold per month.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Revenue:}\quad R &= 364\,q\\
\text{Cost:}\quad C &= 2600 + 260\,q\\
\text{Profit:}\quad P &= R - C = 364\,q - (2600 + 260\,q) = 104\,q - 2600
\end{aligned}
$$

The **break-even point** is the volume at which profit is exactly zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
104\,q - 2600 &= 0 &&\mid +2600\\
104\,q &= 2600 &&\mid :104\\
q &= 25
\end{aligned}
$$

Loop Cycles breaks even at **25 bikes per month**. Below that it makes a loss, above it a profit.

The number 104 has a name: it is the **contribution margin** per unit, the price minus the variable cost, $p - v = 364 - 260$. Each bike sold "contributes" €104 towards the fixed costs. Once 25 bikes have paid off the €2,600, every further bike adds €104 of profit. In general:

$$q_{\text{break-even}} = \frac{F}{p - v}$$

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake: forgetting the brackets around the cost
$364\,q - 2600 + 260\,q$ is wrong: the minus sign must apply to the whole cost, $-(2600 + 260\,q) = -2600 - 260\,q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: an answer that is not a whole number
If the fixed costs rose to €2,800, the break-even volume would be $q = \frac{2800}{104} \approx 26.92$. Loop Cycles cannot sell 26.92 bikes. With 26 bikes it still makes a small loss, so it needs **27 bikes** to break even. When the unknown counts whole things and you need to reach a target, **round up**.
:::

## Target profit: how many, or at what price?

The same equation answers other questions if you set the profit to a target instead of zero.

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: volume for a target profit
How many bikes must Loop Cycles sell to make a profit of €1,560 per month?

$$
\begin{aligned}
104\,q - 2600 &= 1560 &&\mid +2600\\
104\,q &= 4160 &&\mid :104\\
q &= 40
\end{aligned}
$$

**40 bikes per month.** Check: $40 \cdot 104 - 2600 = 4160 - 2600 = 1560$. ✓
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: price for a target profit
Realistically, the workshop can refurbish about 30 bikes a month. Which price $p$ would give a profit of €1,000 at that volume? Now the price is the unknown:

$$
\begin{aligned}
30\,(p - 260) - 2600 &= 1000 &&\mid +2600\\
30\,(p - 260) &= 3600 &&\mid :30\\
p - 260 &= 120 &&\mid +260\\
p &= 380
\end{aligned}
$$

Loop Cycles would have to charge **€380 net** per bike, €16 more than now. Whether customers will pay that is a different question, and it is one that mathematics alone cannot answer.
:::

::: {.voice}
This is my favourite kind of result: the maths gives a clear number, and then the real discussion starts. Would customers pay €380? Could the workshop do 35 bikes instead? A good equation does not make the decision for you. It tells you exactly what you would have to believe for a plan to work.
:::

## More linear equations from everyday business

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: salary with commission
A sales job pays a base salary of €2,000 per month plus 5 % commission on sales. What sales $s$ are needed to earn €2,600?

$$2000 + 0.05\,s = 2600 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0.05\,s = 600 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = \frac{600}{0.05} = 12\,000$$

Sales of **€12,000** per month.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: VAT as an equation
In Session 1 you learnt the rule "net = gross : 1.19". It is just the solution of an equation. If a customer paid €595 including VAT, the net price $x$ satisfies

$$1.19\,x = 595 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{595}{1.19} = 500$$

Many "rules" you have memorised are equations that someone solved for you once. If you forget the rule, set up the equation and solve it yourself.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check yourself

1. Solve $3(x - 4) = x + 6$.

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $3x - 12 = x + 6$, so $2x = 18$ and $x = 9$. Check: $3 \cdot 5 = 15 = 9 + 6$. ✓
   :::

2. A food truck has fixed costs of €1,800 per month. Each meal costs €4 to make and sells for €10 (net). What is the break-even volume?

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   Contribution margin $10 - 4 = 6$. Break-even: $\frac{1800}{6} = 300$ meals per month.
   :::

3. With the same food truck, how many meals are needed for a profit of €2,400?

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $6q - 1800 = 2400$, so $6q = 4200$ and $q = 700$ meals.
   :::

4. A course provider's fixed costs are €5,000, the variable cost per participant is €35 and the price is €120. How many participants are needed to break even?

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $\frac{5000}{120 - 35} = \frac{5000}{85} \approx 58.8$, so **59 participants** (round up).
   :::
:::
